quizTitle: Lightning Brain: Mental Math Speed Academy
description: A full 25-question class that turns strong kids (roughly ages 9-13) into human calculators. Teaches the real techniques speed-mathematicians use: add left-to-right, subtract by counting up, x5/x9 shortcuts, the x11 trick, square two-digit numbers, multiply any two-digit x two-digit with the box method, multiply close-together numbers via a2-b2, and read division backwards. The playground teaches every technique with something to play with and ends in a hard, timed Sprint Arena; the 25 questions climb from quick wins to real challenges.

playground.title: Lightning Brain Academy: Think Like a Human Calculator
playground.intro: You already know your basic facts - this is the next level. These are the actual techniques that let people add 147+138, square 85, or do 47x38 in their head faster than someone can type it into a calculator. Steal all seven, play at every stop, then prove it in the Sprint Arena with real two-digit numbers. Let's go.
playground.outro: That's the full arsenal: add left-to-right, subtract by counting up, lean on x5 and x9 shortcuts, x11 in one slide, square two-digit numbers, box-method any two-digit x two-digit, and read division backwards. None of it is memorising - it's all clever structure. The rest is reps: come back to the Champion Sprint and keep smashing your Best. That's how a normal brain becomes a lightning brain.

stops.title: Technique 1: Add LEFT to Right
stops.tagline: Big parts first. Faster, and you can say the answer as you go.
explain: On paper you add right-to-left, carrying. In your head that's slow and easy to lose. Champions flip it: do the BIG parts first, left to right.
47 + 38? Tens: 40+30 = 70. Ones: 7+8 = 15. Glue: 70+15 = 85. You had 'seventy-something' locked in before you finished - that's the speed.
Slide the numbers; the jump shows the tens leap first, then the ones finishing through a ten.

sim.title: Tens first, then ones
sim.tip: Read it as 40+30, then 7+8. Try 56+27 and 68+25.

stops.smart: Real life: two bills of £47 and £38. The slow person reaches for a phone; you say 'eighty-five' before they unlock it, because you started from the big end.
stops.question: Add left-to-right: 58 + 35. What do you get?

stops.title: Technique 2: Subtract by Counting UP
stops.tagline: Never 'borrow'. Measure the gap through tidy tens.
explain: Two-digit take-away with borrowing is where most people crawl. Drop it. Measure the GAP by counting up from the small number, bridging through tens.
84 - 67? Start at 67. Up to 70 is 3. From 70 up to 84 is 14. Gap = 3+14 = 17. No borrowing, no stress.
Slide the numbers and watch it hop up to a ten first, then finish.

sim.title: Count up the gap
sim.tip: Read 84-67 as 'how far from 67 to 84?'. Try 92-58 and 71-46.

stops.smart: Real life: paying £67 with £80 in notes. The change is just the gap counted up - which is exactly why cashiers say 'and 3 makes 70, and 14 makes 84'.
stops.question: Count up: 73 - 48. What's the gap?
stops.answer: 25. From 48 to 50 is 2, then 50 to 73 is 23, and 2+23=25.

stops.title: Technique 3: x5 and x9 Shortcuts
stops.tagline: x5 is half of x10. x9 is x10 minus one lot.
explain: Two shortcuts that kill whole columns of the times table. x5: multiply by 10 and halve it. 48x5 = 480 halved = 240.
x9: multiply by 10 and take one lot away. 27x9 = 270 - 27 = 243. Way faster than the 9 times table.
Run numbers through the machine to feel x5 and x9, then check with the dot grid's break-apart.

sim.title: The x9 machine
sim.tip: 27x9 = 270 - 27 = 243. Switch your thinking to x5 = half of x10 too.

stops.smart: Real life: 48 stickers at 5p each. Don't grind the 5 times table - think 48x10 = 480, half it = 240p. Halving and 'one lot less' are lightning fast.
stops.question: Use the shortcut: 36 x 5.

stops.title: Technique 4: The x11 Lightning Trick
stops.tagline: Two-digit x 11: split the digits, drop their sum in the middle.
explain: x11 has a trick so clean it feels like cheating. Pull the digits apart and put their SUM in the gap.
If the digit-sum is 10+, carry it: 47x11 -> 4_(11)_7 -> carry the 1 -> 517. Run a few through the machine.

sim.title: The x11 machine
sim.tip: Put in 35 -> 385. Try 26, 52, then 47 (watch the carry to 517).

stops.smart: Real life: 11 weeks saving £35 -> £385, while everyone else reaches for a calculator. Shortcuts like this are the gap between looking slow and looking brilliant.
stops.question: Use the trick: 63 x 11.

stops.title: Technique 5: Square Two-Digit Numbers
stops.tagline: Squaring a number that ends in 5 is almost cheating.
explain: A square is a number times itself: 25² = 25x25. Scary - unless it ends in 5.
Trick for any _5 number: take the tens digit, multiply by the NEXT number up, then stick 25 on the end. 25²: 2x3=6 -> 625. 85²: 8x9=72 -> 7225.
The dot square shows why a square is literally a square: rows = columns.

sim.title: A square is rows = columns
sim.tip: Set rows=columns to see a square (7x7=49). Break-apart still works: 7x7 = 7x5+7x2.

stops.smart: Real life: a 25x25 tile patio. No calculator - 2x3 is 6, slap on 25 -> 625 tiles. People think you're a genius; you just know the pattern.
stops.question: Square it: 45².

stops.title: Technique 6: The Box Method (any 2-digit x 2-digit)
stops.tagline: Split both numbers into tens and ones. Four easy corners, then add.
explain: This is the general technique - it cracks ANY two-digit times two-digit, not just the trick ones. Split each number into tens + ones and multiply the four corners.
Slide both numbers in the box and watch the four pieces - the area really is the answer.

sim.title: Split into four corners
sim.tip: 23x21 = 400+20+60+3 = 483. Slide a and b and watch the four boxes change.

stops.smart: Real life: a car park 23 spaces wide and 21 deep. Break it into a big 20x20 block plus three thin strips - that's how you count a crowd fast, in chunks.
stops.question: Box method: 32 x 21. (30+2)x(20+1).

stops.title: Technique 7: Close-Together Multiplying
stops.tagline: Numbers either side of an easy middle? Use middle² - distance².
explain: A pro move for two numbers that straddle an easy middle by the same amount: (m-d)(m+d) = m² - d².
13x7? Straddle 10, each 3 away: 10² - 3² = 100 - 9 = 91. 18x22? Straddle 20, each 2 away: 400 - 4 = 396.
It also kills almost-squares: 7x9 = 8² - 1 = 63. The dot grid's break-apart shows the everyday version.

sim.title: 8x8, and 7x9 next door
sim.tip: 8x8=64, so 7x9 is one less: 63. Slide rows/cols to 7 and 9 to check.

stops.smart: Real life: a box 13 cans long and 7 wide. Slow way: long multiplication. Fast way: 100 - 9 = 91. One breath.
stops.question: Use the trick: 12 x 8 (straddle 10).

stops.title: Two-Digit Sprint
stops.tagline: No more single digits. Real numbers, 40 seconds.
explain: Techniques are nothing without reps. Here's a pure two-digit add/subtract sprint - exactly where left-to-right and count-up pay off.
Type the answer; the instant it's right the next jumps in. Reach for the technique - don't count.
Your score saves as your Best. Beat yesterday-you.

sim.title: 40s Two-Digit Sprint
sim.tip: Add left-to-right; subtract by counting up. Chase that Best.

stops.smart: A streak of 8+ here means the two-digit tricks are becoming automatic - a genuinely strong skill, not a party trick.
stops.question: What was your best streak on two-digit facts?
stops.answer: Whatever it was - go beat it. These are the numbers that matter in real life.

stops.title: The Champion Sprint
stops.tagline: Everything, including trick facts. 45 seconds. Prove it.
explain: The real arena: two-digit add and subtract, multiplication, x11 trick-facts, and squares - all mixed, 45 seconds.
Grab the right weapon for each: left-to-right, count-up, x5/x9, x11 split, the _5 square, box method, or close-together a²-b².
Beat your Best, then beat it again. This arena is your dojo - live here.

sim.title: Champion Sprint: 2-digit + trick facts
sim.tip: Mixed two-digit +, -, x, x11 and squares. Use the matching technique for each.

stops.smart: Champions aren't the kids who never miss - they're the ones who do the most reps. Every red shake is your brain rewiring. Keep racing.
stops.question: Which technique is still your slowest?
stops.answer: That's your homework. Run a single-skill sprint on just that one until it stops being the slow one.

questions.question: You score 68 points in round one and 57 in round two. What's your total?

hint.title: Add Left-to-Right
hint.subtitle: Big parts first - the champion way to add.

sections.heading: Why the school method is slow in your head
body: On paper you add right-to-left and carry. In your head, carrying is exactly where people stall.
Fast adders start at the BIG end, left to right, so the answer is almost known instantly.

sections.heading: The big idea: tens, then ones
sections.body: 68 + 57: tens 60+50 = 110, ones 8+7 = 15, glue 110+15 = 125. You were sitting on 'a hundred and ten something' before you finished.
sections.note: Add from the left. Lock the big parts first, then adjust with the ones.

sections.heading: Fun fact: world champions add this way
sections.body: At the Mental Calculation World Cup, competitors add ten 10-digit numbers in under a minute - and every one works left-to-right, because starting big lets you say the answer before you finish.
sections.note: World-record mental adders all go left-to-right. The school method is built for paper, not speed.

sections.heading: Where it wins in real life
sections.body: Left-to-right adding is an everyday superpower.
points: Two prices: £68 + £57 -> '125' before they find a phone.
Two game scores or two cricket innings.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body: Out loud, big-end first, no pencil:
points: Say the tens total first, THEN finish with the ones.
Then open the Two-Digit Sprint and chase a streak of 8.

sections.heading: Back to your score
sections.note: Tens first (60+50), then the ones (8+7=15), then glue. Beat the calculator.

questions.question: A snack stand sells 147 drinks before half-time and 138 after. How many altogether?

hint.title: Left-to-Right with Three Digits
hint.subtitle: Hundreds, then tens, then ones.

sections.heading: Same trick, bigger numbers
sections.body: Three digits don't change the method - you just start one column further left.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: Hundreds, then tens, then ones - always left to right.

sections.heading: Fun fact: lightning calculators talk while they add
sections.body: Stage performers begin announcing the leftmost digits of a sum while still working out the rest - only possible because they add from the big end.
sections.note: Starting from the left means you can speak the answer as you go.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Say the hundreds, then tens, then ones.

sections.heading: Back to the snack stand
sections.note: 200... then 40+30... then 7+8=15. Glue them.

questions.question: A game gives 396 coins in level one and 247 in level two. Total coins?

hint.title: Add by Rounding then Adjusting
hint.subtitle: A messy number near a round one? Round, add, then give back.

sections.heading: Spot the 'almost round' number
body: 396 is annoying - but it's only 4 away from 400, which is lovely.
So add 400 instead, then take the extra 4 back at the end. This is called compensation.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: Round up to the easy number, add, then subtract what you borrowed.

sections.heading: Fun fact: your brain loves round numbers
sections.body: Studies of mental arithmetic show people are dramatically faster near 'landmark' numbers like 100 and 1000 - so the trick is to travel via a landmark and adjust.
sections.note: Detour through a round number; it's almost always faster.

sections.heading: Where it shows up
sections.body: Prices ending in 9 are everywhere on purpose.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Say which round number you jumped to.
Then try the same idea on the sprint.

sections.heading: Back to the coins
sections.note: Jump 396 up to 400, add, then give the 4 back.

questions.question: A bus holds 84 people. 67 get on. How many empty seats are left?

hint.title: Subtract by Counting Up
hint.subtitle: Don't take away - measure the gap.

sections.heading: Why borrowing is slow
body: Crossing out and borrowing is where two-digit subtraction falls apart in your head.
Flip it: count UP from the small number to the big one. The gap IS the answer.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.body: 84 - 67: from 67 up to 70 is 3, from 70 up to 84 is 14, total gap 3+14 = 17.
sections.note: Bridge to the next ten, then finish. Add the two hops.

sections.heading: Fun fact: this is how change works
sections.body: Cashiers for centuries gave change by counting UP from the price to the cash given - never by subtracting. It's faster and harder to get wrong.
sections.note: Shops count up: 'and 3 makes 70, and 14 makes 84.'

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body: Count up, bridging through a ten:
points: Say the bridge ('up to 60...') then the rest.

sections.heading: Back to the bus
sections.note: From 67 up to 70, then up to 84. Add the hops.

questions.question: A phone costs 503 coins. You have 298. How many more do you need?

hint.title: Subtract Near a Round Number
hint.subtitle: Both numbers near hundreds? Count up the easy way.

sections.heading: Look for the round numbers hiding inside
body: 298 is almost 300; 503 is just past 500. Use those landmarks.
Count up from 298: to 300 is 2, to 500 is 200, to 503 is 3.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: Count up through every landmark: next ten, next hundred, then the rest.

sections.heading: Fun fact: shopkeepers beat calculators on change
sections.body: Counting up in landmark jumps is so reliable that it was the standard way to give change long before tills did the maths - and it's still faster for a trained brain.
sections.note: Landmarks (tens, hundreds) are stepping stones across the gap.

sections.heading: Where it shows up
points: Points to reach the next level.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Name each landmark you land on.
Then test it in the sprint.

sections.heading: Back to the phone
sections.note: Up to 300, up to 500, then to 503. Add the jumps.

questions.question: A water tank holds 1000 litres. 432 have been used. How many are left?

hint.title: Subtracting from 1000
hint.subtitle: A tidy trick: take each digit from 9, and the last from 10.

sections.heading: Subtracting from 1000 has a shortcut
body: Counting up still works, but there's an even slicker move for 100, 1000, 10000.
Take every digit from 9, except the LAST one, which you take from 10.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: From 1000: 9 minus each digit, but 10 minus the final digit.

sections.heading: Fun fact: this is how old machines subtracted
sections.body: Early mechanical calculators subtracted by adding the 'nines complement' - exactly this take-from-9 trick - because adding is easier to build than subtracting. Computers still use a version of it today.
sections.note: 'Complements' let machines (and you) turn subtraction into something easier.

sections.heading: Where it shows up
points: Litres or grams left in a full container.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Say the digits out loud as you flip them.

sections.heading: Back to the tank
sections.note: 9-4, 9-3, 10-2. Read off the three digits.

questions.question: A pack has 48 stickers. You buy 5 packs. How many stickers?

hint.title: x5 = Half of x10
hint.subtitle: The easiest multiplication shortcut there is.

sections.heading: x10 is free, so make x5 from it
body: Multiplying by 10 is just adding a zero - effortless. And 5 is half of 10.
So to multiply by 5: multiply by 10, then halve.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: x5 = (x10) then halve. Always.

sections.heading: Fun fact: clocks run on fives
sections.body: Every number on a clock face is 5 minutes apart, which is why we read time in fives so fast - your brain has been practising x5 since you learned to tell the time.
sections.note: Telling time is secret x5 practice you've done for years.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Say the x10 answer first, then halve.
Then turn on multiplication in the sprint.

sections.heading: Back to the stickers
sections.note: 48 x 10 then halve.

questions.question: A bracelet uses 27 beads. You make 9 bracelets. How many beads?

hint.title: x9 = x10 Minus One Lot
hint.subtitle: Nine is just ten with one taken back.

sections.heading: Don't grind the 9 times table
body: 9 is one less than 10. So nine lots of something is ten lots minus one lot.
Multiply by 10, then subtract the number once.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: x9 = (x10) minus one lot of the number.

sections.heading: Fun fact: the 9 times table digits add to 9
sections.body: Look at 9, 18, 27, 36, 45... each answer's digits add up to 9 (1+8, 2+7, 3+6). It's a built-in self-check that the result is right.
sections.note: If a 'x9' answer's digits don't add to 9 (or a multiple), you slipped.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Check each with the digit-sum trick.
Then race it in the sprint.

sections.heading: Back to the beads
sections.note: 270 minus one lot of 27.

questions.question: You save 35 coins a day for 11 days. How many coins?

hint.title: The x11 Trick (no carry)
hint.subtitle: Split the digits, drop their sum in the middle.

sections.heading: Eleven is secretly the friendliest multiplier
body: 11 = 10 + 1, so n x 11 is n x 10 plus one more n. That powers a clean shortcut.
For a two-digit number: write the digits apart, sum in the gap.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: Two-digit x 11 = first digit, (sum of digits), last digit.

sections.heading: Fun fact: it scales up
sections.body: The same idea gives x101 and x1001 (the number plus a shifted copy of itself), which is how performers multiply huge numbers on stage in seconds.
sections.note: x11, x101, x1001 are all 'a number plus a shifted copy'.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Say first digit, middle sum, last digit.
Then switch on x11 in the Champion Sprint.

sections.heading: Back to the coins
sections.note: 3, then 3+5, then 5.

questions.question: A theatre has 11 rows with 47 seats each. Total seats?

hint.title: The x11 Trick (with carry)
hint.subtitle: When the digit-sum hits 10, carry it left.

sections.heading: Most x11 problems need the carry
body: The split-and-sum trick is easy until the two digits add to 10 or more.
Then the middle spills over and carries left, just like normal addition.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.body: 47 x 11: digits 4 and 7 add to 11. Write 4 _(11)_ 7; carry the 1 so the 4 becomes 5 -> 517.
sections.note: Digit-sum 10+? Put the units in the middle, carry the 1 to the left digit.

sections.heading: Fun fact: the carry is the only hard part
sections.body: Surveys of mental-math learners find the no-carry x11 is mastered almost instantly; the carry is the one step worth drilling - so that's exactly where reps pay off.
sections.note: Drill the carrying x11 cases; the rest is already easy.

sections.heading: Where it shows up
points: 11 rows of seats in a hall.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Then chase a streak with x11 on in the sprint.

sections.heading: Back to the theatre
sections.note: 4 and 7 make 11; carry into the 4.

questions.question: A floor needs 36 boxes of tiles with 25 tiles per box. How many tiles?

hint.title: x25 = Quarter of x100
hint.subtitle: Twenty-five is a quarter of a hundred.

sections.heading: Lean on 100
body: x100 is free (two zeros). And 25 is a quarter of 100.
So x25 = multiply by 100, then halve twice (a quarter).

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: x25 = (x100) then halve twice. Or box-method it.

sections.heading: Fun fact: money is built on 25
sections.body: Quarters (25 of something) appear in coins, in 'quarter past', and in 25% = one quarter. Your brain already splits things into quarters all the time.
sections.note: 25 is just 'a quarter', and quarters are everywhere.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Or check with the box method.

sections.heading: Back to the tiles
sections.note: 3600, halved, halved again.

questions.question: A square garden is 25 metres on each side. What's its area (25 x 25)?

hint.title: Squaring Numbers Ending in 5
hint.subtitle: Tens digit times the next number, then 25.

sections.heading: Squares ending in 5 are a free win
body: A square is a number times itself. For anything ending in 5 there's a one-line trick.
Take the tens digit, multiply by the NEXT whole number, then write 25 on the end.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.body: 25²: tens digit 2, next number 3, so 2x3 = 6, then 25 -> 625.
sections.note: _5 squared = (tens)x(tens+1) then 25.

sections.heading: Fun fact: why the trick works
sections.body: (10t+5)² = 100t² + 100t + 25 = 100·t(t+1) + 25 - which is exactly 't times t+1' followed by 25. The algebra guarantees it every time.
sections.note: It's not luck - the algebra forces the '25 on the end'.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Then turn squares on in the sprint.

questions.question: What is 85 squared (85 x 85)?

hint.title: Bigger _5 Squares
hint.subtitle: The same trick handles 85 as easily as 25.

sections.heading: It scales to any number ending in 5
body: The tens-times-next trick doesn't care how big the tens digit is.
85: tens digit is 8, the next number is 9.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: 8x9 then 25. The '25' on the end never changes.

sections.heading: Fun fact: human calculators square huge numbers
sections.body: Record holders have squared random 5-digit and even 6-digit numbers in their heads - they chain shortcuts like this one together rather than 'calculating' the long way.
sections.note: Big mental feats are many small tricks stacked, not brute force.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Notice the answer always ends in 25.

questions.question: A car park is 23 spaces wide and 21 deep. How many spaces (23 x 21)?

hint.title: The Box Method
hint.subtitle: Any 2-digit x 2-digit: four corners, then add.

sections.heading: The all-purpose multiplication technique
body: The tricks are great when they fit, but the box method works for ANY two-digit times two-digit.
Split each number into tens + ones and multiply the four corners.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: Tens x tens, tens x ones, ones x tens, ones x ones - then add.

sections.heading: Fun fact: it's the same as the grid you'll meet in algebra
sections.body: The box method is exactly how older students multiply brackets like (x+3)(x+1). Learn it now with numbers and algebra will feel familiar later.
sections.note: Today's number box is tomorrow's algebra grid.

sections.heading: Where it shows up
points: Car parks, seating blocks, tiled floors.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Write the four products before adding.
Slide the box widget to check.

questions.question: A book has 47 lines per page and you read 38 pages. How many lines (47 x 38)?

hint.title: Box Method with Carries
hint.subtitle: Bigger corners - just add carefully.

sections.heading: Same method, bigger pieces
body: When both numbers are large, the four corners are bigger but the method is identical.
Take your time on the addition - that's where slips happen.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: Biggest corner first (40x30); it anchors the answer's size.

sections.heading: Fun fact: estimate first to catch mistakes
sections.body: Pros glance at 47x38 and think '~50x40 = 2000', so they know the answer must be near 2000. If your four corners sum to 786, you'd instantly know something's wrong.
sections.note: Always estimate first: 47x38 is roughly 50x40 = 2000.

sections.heading: Where it shows up
points: Lines in a book, words on pages.
Seats in a big arena block.
Items per box times many boxes.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Say the ~estimate before the exact answer.

questions.question: A wall is 64 bricks long and 56 bricks high. How many bricks (64 x 56)?

hint.title: Box Method: the Tough Ones
hint.subtitle: Two big numbers, no special trick - and that's fine.

sections.heading: When no shortcut fits, the box always works
body: 64 and 56 don't end in 5, aren't near each other - no special trick. The box method just powers through.
This is the safety net behind all the flashy tricks.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: Even the 'hard' ones are just four easy products added up.

sections.heading: A shortcut peek
sections.body: 64 and 56 straddle 60, each 4 away - so a²-b² also works:

sections.heading: Fun fact: more than one road to the answer
sections.body: Strong mental mathematicians often see two or three routes to the same product and pick the easiest in the moment - here, both the box and a²-b² land on 3584.
sections.note: If two different methods agree, you can trust the answer.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body: Box method (and try a²-b² if they straddle):
points: Notice which ones straddle a round middle.

questions.question: A tray holds 13 rows of 7 muffins. How many muffins (13 x 7)?

hint.title: Close-Together Multiplying
hint.subtitle: Straddle an easy middle, then middle squared minus distance squared.

sections.heading: Some 'hard' products are secretly easy
body: 13 x 7 isn't a friendly table fact - but 13 and 7 sit either side of 10, each 3 away.
When numbers straddle an easy middle by the same amount, squaring beats multiplying.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: Same distance either side of a middle: answer = middle² - distance².

sections.heading: Fun fact: this identity guards your secrets
sections.body: a²-b² = (a-b)(a+b) is over a thousand years old and still vital: the difficulty of factoring big numbers (the reverse of this) is part of how online encryption protects your messages.
sections.note: One little identity runs from mental tricks to internet security.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Say middle and distance before answering.

sections.heading: Back to the muffins
sections.note: Middle 10, distance 3: 100 - 9.

questions.question: A box is 18 cans wide and 22 cans long. How many cans (18 x 22)?

hint.title: Straddling a Bigger Middle
hint.subtitle: The a2-b2 trick works around any round number.

sections.heading: The middle doesn't have to be 10
body: 18 and 22 straddle 20, each 2 away. So the easy middle is 20.
The bigger the round middle, the more impressive the shortcut looks.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: Spot the round number they straddle; that's your middle.

sections.heading: Fun fact: it makes huge products look effortless
sections.body: 97 x 103 looks terrifying, but it straddles 100: 10000 - 9 = 9991. A four-digit answer in one second - that's the power of choosing the right middle.
sections.note: Near 100? The shortcut gives four-digit answers instantly.

sections.heading: Where it shows up
points: Pricing just under/over a round number.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Then check on the box widget.

sections.heading: Back to the cans
sections.note: Middle 20, distance 2: 400 - 4.

questions.question: A hall has 47 rows of 53 chairs. How many chairs (47 x 53)?

hint.title: a2-b2 with Big Numbers
hint.subtitle: 47 x 53 becomes 2500 minus 9.

sections.heading: This is where the trick shines brightest
body: 47 x 53 by long multiplication is real work. But they straddle 50, each 3 away.
Suddenly it's just '50 squared minus 3 squared'.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: 50² is easy (2500); subtract the small square.

sections.heading: Fun fact: knowing your squares unlocks this
sections.body: Because the trick needs middle², people who memorise squares of 10, 20, ... 100 can multiply a huge range of pairs instantly. Squares are a small investment with a giant payoff.
sections.note: Learn the round-number squares; they unlock hundreds of products.

sections.heading: Where it shows up
points: Fields and plots near a round size.

questions.question: A garden has 7 rows of 48 carrots. How many carrots (7 x 48)?

hint.title: Break Apart the Big Number
hint.subtitle: Split a 2-digit number into friendly chunks, then add.

sections.heading: One-digit times two-digit? Split the big one
body: 7 x 48 looks awkward, but 48 = 40 + 8, and both are easy to multiply by 7.
Do each piece, then add - this is the distributive law in action.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: Split the two-digit number into tens and ones, multiply each, add.

sections.heading: Fun fact: this is multiplication's backbone
sections.body: Every multiplication method - the box, long multiplication, even how computers multiply - is really 'break into parts, multiply, add'. Master this and you understand them all.
sections.note: Split-multiply-add is the engine inside every multiplication method.

questions.question: A cinema has 6 screens with 84 seats each. How many seats (6 x 84)?

hint.title: Break Apart, or Round and Adjust
hint.subtitle: Two routes to 6 x 84 - pick your favourite.

sections.heading: Two good ways here
body: You can split 84 into 80 + 4, or you can round 84 up to a friendlier number and adjust.
Strong mental maths is about choosing the easier road.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: Split into tens+ones, OR round to a friendly number and give back.

sections.heading: Fun fact: experts keep several routes ready
sections.body: Research on 'flexible' calculators shows the fastest people don't use one fixed method - they pick the strategy that fits the numbers in front of them. Flexibility, not a single trick, is the real skill.
sections.note: The best mental mathematicians are flexible, not robotic.

questions.question: 91 stickers are shared equally among 7 friends. How many each (91 ÷ 7)?

hint.title: Division is Multiplication Backwards
hint.subtitle: Don't divide - ask a times-table question.

sections.heading: Division isn't a new monster
body: 91 ÷ 7 is secretly asking '7 times WHAT makes 91?'.
Every division is a multiplication fact read from the other end.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.body: From the close-together trick you may know 7 x 13 = 91 (13x7 = 100-9). So 91 ÷ 7 = 13.
sections.note: Turn 'a ÷ b' into 'b times what makes a?'.

sections.heading: Fun fact: strong tables = strong division
sections.body: There's no separate 'division table' to learn. Kids with fast times tables are automatically fast at division, because it's the very same facts in reverse.
sections.note: Master multiplication and you get division for free.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body: Say each as a times question:
points: '8 times what is 72?' and so on.
Then turn on division in the sprint.

sections.heading: Back to the stickers
sections.note: '7 times what is 91?'

questions.question: 96 cookies go equally into 8 boxes. How many per box (96 ÷ 8)?

hint.title: Divide by Halving
hint.subtitle: ÷8 is just halve, halve, halve.

sections.heading: A second division superpower
body: Dividing by 2 is just halving - your brain does it instantly.
8 = 2x2x2, so dividing by 8 is halving three times in a row.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.note: ÷4 = halve twice. ÷8 = halve three times.

sections.heading: Fun fact: computers ONLY halve and double
sections.body: Deep inside every chip, division is done by repeated halving in binary (0s and 1s). The halving trick you just used is, at heart, how machines divide too.
sections.note: Halving and doubling are powerful enough to run every computer on Earth.

sections.heading: Where it shows up
points: Cutting a recipe in half (or quarters).

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Count how many halvings you used.

sections.heading: Back to the cookies
sections.note: Halve 96 three times.

questions.question: 84 players form teams of 6. How many teams (84 ÷ 6)?

hint.title: Divide by Chunking
hint.subtitle: Take away easy lots until you've used it all up.

sections.heading: When the fact isn't instant, chunk it
body: 84 ÷ 6 isn't a memorised fact, so build it from easy lots of 6.
Ten 6s is 60 - a friendly chunk to start with.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.body: 84 ÷ 6: ten 6s = 60 (10 teams), leaving 24. Four 6s = 24 (4 teams). Total 10 + 4 = 14.
sections.note: Pull off a big easy chunk (like 10 lots), then finish the rest.

sections.heading: Fun fact: chunking is real long division
sections.body: The 'chunking' method is exactly what long division does, just written differently - you repeatedly subtract multiples of the divisor. It also handles leftovers as remainders.
sections.note: Chunking is long division in friendly clothing.

sections.heading: Back to the teams
sections.note: Ten 6s (60), then four more 6s (24).

questions.question: 738 books are shared equally onto 9 shelves. How many per shelf (738 ÷ 9)?

hint.title: Big Division, Two Smart Ways
hint.subtitle: Chunk it - or use the digit-sum check for 9.

sections.heading: Bigger numbers, same toolkit
body: 738 ÷ 9 looks scary, but chunking handles it, and 9 has a special helper.
First, a sanity check: a number divides exactly by 9 only if its digits add to a multiple of 9. 7+3+8 = 18 -> yes, it divides cleanly.

sections.heading: The big idea (chunking)
sections.body: 738 ÷ 9: eighty 9s = 720 (80 shelves' worth), leaving 18. Two 9s = 18. Total 80 + 2 = 82.
sections.note: Pull off a big chunk (eighty 9s = 720), then finish the small rest.

sections.heading: Check it backwards
sections.body: Division and multiplication are inverses, so verify:

sections.heading: Fun fact: the digit-sum test is ancient
sections.body: 'Casting out nines' - checking answers using digit sums - was used by mathematicians over a thousand years ago to catch arithmetic mistakes, long before calculators. 7+3+8 = 18, and 8+2 = 10... the nine-ness lines up.
sections.note: Add the digits: if they sum to a multiple of 9, the number divides by 9.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
points: Add the digits first to confirm it's clean.

sections.heading: Back to the books
sections.note: Eighty 9s = 720, then two more 9s = 18. Check: 82 x 9 = 738.
